facts.text: The applicants’ seventeen close relatives were members of an outlawed organisation in Turkey, namely the Maoist Communist Party (MKP).

anchor.surface_text: 5.  The applicants’ seventeen close relatives were members of an outlawed organisation in Turkey, namely the Maoist Communist Party (hereinafter “the MKP”).

facts.text: On various dates since the 1970s criminal proceedings had been brought against the relatives for membership of outlawed organisations and for carrying out activities on their behalf.

anchor.surface_text: On various dates since the 1970s criminal proceedings had been brought against the relatives for membership of a number of outlawed organisations and for carrying out activities on behalf of those organisations.

facts.text: The relatives had spent various periods of time in prisons, and after release some had left Turkey and settled in different European countries.

anchor.surface_text: They had spent various periods of time in prisons, and after their release some of them had left Turkey and settled in different countries in Europe.

facts.text: In early June 2005 the seventeen relatives began arriving in a rural area near Ovacık, Tunceli, to hold a meeting of their organisation.

anchor.surface_text: 6.  In early June 2005 the seventeen relatives began arriving in a rural area within the administrative jurisdiction of the town of Ovacık, near the city of Tunceli, in order to hold a meeting of their organisation.

facts.text: They were all killed in that area by members of the security forces on 17 and 18 June 2005.

anchor.surface_text: They were all killed in that area by members of the security forces on 17 and 18 June 2005.

facts.text: The applicants alleged that the killing of seventeen of their relatives by soldiers and the subsequent exhibiting of their bodies in a car park breached Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention.

anchor.surface_text: 3.  The applicants alleged, in particular, that the killing of seventeen of their relatives by soldiers and the subsequent exhibiting of their bodies in a car park had been in breach of Articles 2 and 3 of the Convention.

facts.text: At around 9 p.m. on 17 June 2005 some applicants heard on television news that nine MKP members had been killed by soldiers in Ovacık and armed clashes were continuing.

anchor.surface_text: 9.  At around 9 p.m. on 17 June 2005 some of the applicants heard on the television news that nine MKP members had been killed by soldiers in Ovacık and that armed clashes were continuing.

facts.text: The following day family members went to Ovacık District Gendarmerie Command seeking information; a lawyer was told by the prosecutor that seventeen people had been killed.

anchor.surface_text: 10.  The following day a number of family members, suspecting that their relatives might be among those who had been killed, went to the Ovacık District Gendarmerie Command to seek more information. When they failed to obtain any information there a lawyer representing one of the families went to see the local prosecutor. The prosecutor told the lawyer that seventeen people had been killed.

facts.text: Families were taken to a nearby military base to identify seventeen bodies placed in the car park; most bodies were naked and identification was incomplete that day.

anchor.surface_text: 11.  The families were then taken to a nearby military base to identify the seventeen bodies, which had been placed in the car park of the military base. The families noted that most of the bodies were naked. As the faces and bodies of the deceased had been destroyed beyond recognition, it was not possible to complete the identification process that day.

facts.text: After identification and autopsies, the bodies were handed over to families for burial.

anchor.surface_text: 12.  When all the bodies had been identified and autopsies carried out on them they were handed over to the families for burial.

facts.text: Photographs and video footage taken by families while bodies were prepared for burial showed very extensive injuries on the bodies of the seventeen.

anchor.surface_text: 13.  The photographs and video footage taken by the families while the bodies were being prepared for burial were submitted to the Court. Very extensive injuries on the bodies of the seventeen can be seen in the footage.

facts.text: The Government submitted that the applicants’ relatives were members of the MKP terrorist organisation and some had entered Turkey illegally to participate in a meeting in Tunceli.

anchor.surface_text: 15.  The applicants’ relatives were members of the MKP terrorist organisation and some of them had entered Turkey illegally in order to participate in a meeting of that organisation in Tunceli.

facts.text: On 17 June 2005 a patrolling helicopter found the terrorist group near Tunceli; the group opened fire on the helicopter.

anchor.surface_text: After receiving intelligence reports, a patrolling helicopter found the terrorist group in an area near Tunceli on 17 June 2005. The terrorist group opened fire on the helicopter.

facts.text: Security forces arrived to arrest the group; at 5 p.m. on 17 June 2005 they encountered the group, who despite warnings to surrender opened fire and injured a soldier.

anchor.surface_text: After determining the location of the group the security forces arrived in the area to arrest them. At 5 p.m. the security forces encountered the group. Despite warnings to surrender issued by the security forces, the terrorists opened fire and injured a soldier.

facts.text: At 9 a.m. on 18 June 2005 the armed clash ended; alongside the bodies, weapons and ammunition were found; three terrorists were apprehended alive and arrested.

anchor.surface_text: At 9 a.m. on 18 June 2005 the armed clash between the security forces and the terrorists ended. Alongside the bodies of the terrorists the security forces found, amongst other things, a number of automatic rifles and ammunition. Three terrorists were apprehended alive and arrested.

facts.text: On 18 June 2005 just after the clash ended, the prosecutor arrived at the incident area, conducted an on-site inspection, prepared an incident report, and opened an investigation concerning the deaths.

anchor.surface_text: On the same day, just after the armed clash ended, the prosecutor arrived at the incident area, conducted an on-site inspection, prepared an incident report, and opened an investigation concerning the deaths of the seventeen terrorists.

facts.text: The prosecutor ordered destruction of material which had no evidential or economic value.

anchor.surface_text: The prosecutor then ordered the destruction of the material which had no evidential or economic value.

facts.text: On 18 June 2005 between 9.30 a.m. and 2.30 p.m. the bodies and everything else found were photographed.

anchor.surface_text: On 18 June 2005 between 9.30 a.m. and 2.30 p.m. the bodies and everything else found were photographed.

facts.text: On 29 June 2005, at the request of the relatives, the prosecutor asked the Forensic Medicine Institute to examine the clothes and bodies to establish whether security forces had opened fire from a distance without warning.

anchor.surface_text: On 29 June 2005, at the request of the relatives of the deceased, the prosecutor asked the Forensic Medicine Institute to examine the clothes and bodies of the deceased with a view to establishing whether the security forces had opened fire from a distance without issuing any warning to surrender.

facts.text: On 1 July 2005 the Forensic Laboratories of the Police in Diyarbakır released a ballistic report stating that sixteen of the seventeen terrorists had actively fired at the security forces during the clashes.

anchor.surface_text: On 1 July 2005 the Forensic Laboratories of the Police in Diyarbakır released the ballistic report, which stated that sixteen of the seventeen terrorists had actively fired at the security forces during the armed clashes.

facts.text: According to the Ovacık District Gendarmerie Command report of 18 June 2005, security forces started a military operation on 15 June 2005 based on intelligence about MKP members planning a meeting near Mercan Mountains.

anchor.surface_text: 22.  According to a report prepared by three non-commissioned officers from the Ovacık District Gendarmerie Command on 18 June 2005 (hereafter “the Ovacık report”), intelligence obtained by the security forces suggested that members of the MKP were planning to have a meeting in mid-June in an area in the vicinity of the Mercan Mountains, near the border between Tunceli and Erzincan provinces. Security forces from Erzincan and Tunceli subsequently started a military operation in the area on 15 June 2005.

facts.text: At around 5 p.m. on 17 June 2005 security forces encountered armed members of the organisation, asked them to surrender, but they responded with fire and an armed clash ensued.

anchor.surface_text: At around 5 p.m. on 17 June 2005 the security forces conducting the operation came across a group of “armed members of the organisation” and asked them to surrender. However, “the members of the organisation” responded with fire and an armed clash ensued.

facts.text: During the first fire opened by the terrorists a soldier was injured on the upper leg and airlifted to hospital by helicopter.

anchor.surface_text: During the first fire opened by “the terrorists” a soldier was injured on the upper leg and airlifted to hospital by helicopter.

facts.text: The clashes continued until the following day due to mountainous terrain and refusal to surrender; at around 10 a.m. the next day the fire stopped and a search recovered fifteen male and two female terrorists' bodies.

anchor.surface_text: As the area was mountainous with many caves and in some places covered with snow, and as the “members of the illegal organisation” refused to surrender and opened intense fire, the clashes continued until the following day. At around 10 a.m. the following day the fire directed at the security forces stopped and then a search was conducted by members of the security forces. The bodies of fifteen male and two female “terrorists” were recovered.

facts.text: The bodies and weapons recovered were taken by helicopter to the Ovacık District Gendarmerie Command as instructed by the public prosecutor.

anchor.surface_text: “As instructed by the public prosecutor”, the bodies and weapons recovered in the area were then taken by helicopter to the Ovacık District Gendarmerie Command.

facts.text: According to the Kemah report of 18 June 2005, outlawed terrorist organisations had set up camp in the area and were in contact with three men from Sarıyazı village who provided assistance.

anchor.surface_text: 25.  Another military report was drawn up on 18 June 2005 by the officer in charge of the District Gendarmerie Command of the neighbouring town of Kemah, and eleven gendarmes who had taken an active part in the operation (hereafter the “Kemah report”). The report states that “outlawed terrorist organisations had set up camp” in the area and that its members had been travelling between Erzincan city centre and Sarıyazı village. There was evidence and information showing that members of the terrorist organisation were in contact with three men from Sarıyazı village who were providing them with assistance.

facts.text: On 8 a.m. on 17 June 2005 two of the three men were apprehended and questioned; one admitted helping armed men by supplying food, transport, and guidance.

anchor.surface_text: At 8 a.m. on 17 June 2005 two of the three men in question were apprehended and questioned by the soldiers. When they denied the allegations against them, the soldiers told them that the mobile telephone belonging to Ali Rıza Sabur – one of the applicants’ deceased relatives – was being intercepted and that the security forces were therefore aware that they had been in contact with members of the illegal organisation who had arrived in the area recently. One of the two men then told the soldiers that he had seen a number of armed men in the area and that he had subsequently helped them by supplying them with food and transport and by providing guidance about the local area.

facts.text: The armed men were spotted in a river bed from armed Cobra-type military helicopters at 11 a.m.; one opened fire, nine were killed in the ensuing clash.

anchor.surface_text: The soldiers then asked for a military helicopter and went to that area with the man to look for the applicants’ relatives. The armed men were spotted in a river bed from armed Cobra-type military helicopters at 11 a.m. When one of the armed men noticed the helicopter, he opened fire and an armed clash ensued during which nine of the armed men were killed.

facts.text: At 4.30 p.m. on 17 June 2005 soldiers came under intense fire, another armed clash ensued and continued until 9 a.m. on 18 June 2005.

anchor.surface_text: At 4.30 p.m. the same day a number of soldiers taking security measures in the area came under intense fire as a result of which another armed clash ensued and continued until 9 a.m. the following morning, that is 18 June 2005.

facts.text: After the operations ended, eight more bodies were recovered with weapons; one of the three men who had been arrested identified the bodies as those he and his friends had helped.

anchor.surface_text: After the operations ended the bodies of eight more people – two of whom were female – were recovered together with their weapons. One of the three men, who had been apprehended the previous morning and had assisted the soldiers in locating the applicants’ relatives, was with the soldiers at that time and identified the bodies as the persons whom he and his two friends had helped after their arrival in the area.

facts.text: The incident took place on the border between the Ovacık and Kemah districts; the Ovacık prosecutor was informed and instructed soldiers to take bodies and belongings to Ovacık.

anchor.surface_text: The report further states that the incident took place on the border between the Ovacık and Kemah districts. The Ovacık prosecutor was then informed about the operation and instructed the soldiers to take the bodies of the seventeen and their belongings to the town of Ovacık.

facts.text: On 18 June 2005 a press release by the Gendarmerie Headquarters stated that seventeen terrorists were recovered dead and three terrorists apprehended alive during the operations.

anchor.surface_text: 27.  On 18 June 2005 a press release was issued by the Gendarmerie Headquarters in Ankara, stating that “seventeen terrorists were recovered dead and three terrorists were apprehended alive” during the operations.

facts.text: The Ovacık prosecutor on 18 June 2005 reported that the area where the relatives were killed was not safe, so bodies were brought to Ovacık by military helicopter and placed in the car park.

anchor.surface_text: 29.  According to a report drawn up by the Ovacık prosecutor on 18 June 2005, the area where the applicants’ relatives had been killed was not safe and therefore it was not possible for the prosecutor to go there to examine the bodies. Thus, a decision was taken to bring the bodies to the town of Ovacık in a military helicopter. When they were brought to the Ovacık District Gendarmerie Command the bodies were placed in the car park reserved for military vehicles.

facts.text: The prosecutor and two doctors examined the bodies at the car park, noted all seventeen were clothed, instructed clothes be removed for examination, and photographed bodies clothed and unclothed.

anchor.surface_text: The Ovacık prosecutor, assisted by two doctors, arrived at the car park and examined the bodies. The prosecutor noted that all seventeen were clothed and instructed that the clothes be removed for the examinations to be carried out. The bodies were also photographed, both with their clothes on and after they were taken off.

facts.text: The prosecutor and doctors noted extensive injuries on the bodies; sixteen identity documents were found in clothes; ten belonged to deceased, six were in names of others.

anchor.surface_text: The prosecutor and the doctors noted in their report the extensive injuries they observed on the bodies. A search was carried out of the clothes, in which sixteen identity documents were found. The prosecutor decided to keep the number tags on the bodies in place as he suspected that some of the identity papers might be forged. It was later established that ten of the identity papers belonged to the deceased and the remaining six identity documents were in the names of other people.

facts.text: Two doctors concluded all seventeen died from injuries caused by bullets and shrapnel; detailed autopsies were necessary.

anchor.surface_text: The two doctors concluded that all seventeen had died as a result of injuries caused by bullets and shrapnel, but considered it necessary to have detailed autopsies carried out.

facts.text: Bodies were handed to a gendarme non-commissioned officer who took them to the Forensic Medicine Institute’s Malatya branch at around 8 p.m. the same day.

anchor.surface_text: The bodies were then handed over to a gendarme non-commissioned officer, who took them to the Forensic Medicine Institute’s nearest branch in the city of Malatya at around 8 p.m. the same day.

facts.text: On the evening of 18 June 2005 three people who claimed to know some deceased identified six bodies at the Forensic Medicine Institute’s Malatya Branch.

anchor.surface_text: The same evening three people who claimed to know some of the deceased arrived at the Forensic Medicine Institute’s Malatya Branch and identified the bodies of Cafer Cangöz, Aydın Hanbayat, Ökkeş Karaoğlu, Okan Ünsal, İbrahim Akdeniz and Gülnaz Yıldız.

facts.text: Forensic pathologists started autopsies on the evening of 18 June 2005 and completed them at 6.30 a.m. the following morning in presence of Malatya prosecutor.

anchor.surface_text: The same evening forensic pathologists started carrying out the autopsies; they completed their examinations at 6.30 the following morning. A detailed verbatim report of the actions taken during the autopsies was prepared in the presence of the Malatya prosecutor.

facts.text: Blood and urine samples were taken to verify alcohol or drug use; swabs were taken from hands for ballistic examinations; bullets and shrapnel were sent for analysis; fingerprints were taken for identification.

anchor.surface_text: Blood and urine samples taken from the bodies were sent for further analysis to verify whether the deceased had consumed alcohol or used drugs. Swabs were taken from their hands and sent for ballistic examinations with a view to establishing whether they had any gunpowder residue on their hands. Bullets and shrapnel found in the bodies were also sent for further analysis. Fingerprints were taken for identification purposes.

facts.text: According to the autopsy report, eight deceased were killed by explosives, three by bullets, and six by both explosives and bullets.

anchor.surface_text: According to the findings of the forensic pathologists which are set out in the autopsy report, eight of the deceased had been killed by explosives, three of them by bullets, and the remaining six by both explosives and bullets.

facts.text: The forensic pathologists noted that with one exception all deceased had been stripped of their clothes and clothes of thirteen of the sixteen remaining had not been provided for examination.

anchor.surface_text: The forensic pathologists considered that to establish the distances from which the seventeen persons had been shot, further examinations had to be conducted on their clothes. They noted, however, that with one exception all the deceased had been stripped of their clothes and that the clothes belonging to thirteen of the remaining sixteen had not been provided.

facts.text: On 21 June 2005 the Ovacık prosecutor requested a copy of investigation documents relating to arrest of three men who helped the applicants’ relatives; the Kemah prosecutor forwarded a copy.

anchor.surface_text: On 21 June 2005 the Ovacık prosecutor wrote to his opposite number in Kemah and requested a copy of the investigation documents relating to the arrest of the three men (see paragraphs 25-26 above). According to the documents submitted to the Court, the Kemah prosecutor complied with that request and forwarded a copy of his investigation file to the Ovacık prosecutor.

facts.text: On 9 June 2005 security forces obtained authorisation from a judge to intercept the applicants’ relatives’ mobile telephones; conversations with locals were intercepted between 9 and 17 June 2005.

anchor.surface_text: It appears from the Kemah prosecutor’s file that on 9 June 2005 the security forces had obtained authorisation from a judge to intercept the applicants’ relatives’ mobile telephones, and telephone conversations some of the applicants’ relatives had had with a number of local people, including the men who were subsequently arrested for providing them with logistical support, were intercepted by the authorities between 9 and 17 June 2005.

facts.text: On 21 June 2005 the Ovacık prosecutor asked the District Gendarmerie Command to send weapons and ammunition recovered with bodies to Regional Forensic Laboratories for examination.

anchor.surface_text: On 21 June 2005 the Ovacık prosecutor also asked the Ovacık District Gendarmerie Command to send the weapons and the ammunition recovered together with the bodies of the applicants’ relatives to the Regional Forensic Laboratories with a view to establishing whether the rifles had been used in any other previous incident and whether the 23 G3 spent cartridges and the 45 Kalashnikov spent cartridges had been discharged from the G3 and the Kalashnikov rifles found together with the bodies and whether they had thus been used in the armed clash.

facts.text: On 19 and 20 June 2005 most bodies were formally identified by family members and burial certificates issued.

anchor.surface_text: On 19 and 20 June 2005 most of the bodies were formally identified by their family members and burial certificates were issued.

facts.text: On 22 June 2005 three deceased were formally identified after fingerprint examination at Malatya Police Headquarters.

anchor.surface_text: On 22 June 2005 three of the deceased, namely Cafer Cangöz, Berna Saygılı-Ünsal and Ökkeş Karaoğlu, were formally identified after an examination of their fingerprints was conducted at the Malatya Police Headquarters.

facts.text: On 22 June 2005 the Ovacık prosecutor was provided with the medical report of the soldier injured during the operation, who was treated in a military hospital between 18 and 30 June 2005.

anchor.surface_text: The same day the Ovacık prosecutor was provided with the report pertaining to the medical examination of the soldier who had been injured during the operation and airlifted to hospital (see paragraph 22 above). According to the report, the soldier in question had been kept in a military hospital in Elazığ between 18 and 30 June 2005 for the “injury to the skin of and a foreign object on the left femur, which is not life-threatening and which can be treated with a simple medical intervention”.

anchor.surface_text: The Court reiterates that the text of Article 2 of the Convention, read as a whole, demonstrates that paragraph 2 does not primarily define instances where it is permitted to intentionally kill an individual, but describes situations where it is permitted to “use force” which may result, as an unintended outcome, in the deprivation of life. The use of force, however, must be no more than “absolutely necessary” for the achievement of any of the purposes set out in subparagraphs (a), (b) or (c). In this respect the use of the term “absolutely necessary” in Article 2 § 2 indicates that a stricter and more compelling test of necessity must be employed than that normally applicable when determining whether State action is “necessary in a democratic society” under paragraph 2 of Articles 8-11 of the Convention. In particular, the force used must be strictly proportionate to the achievement of the aims set out in sub-paragraphs 2 (a), (b) and (c) of Article 2 of the Convention (see McCann and Others v. the United Kingdom, 27 September 1995, §§ 148-149, Series A no. 324).

concepts.interpretation: The Court applies a strict necessity and proportionality test under Article 2 § 2, requiring force to be no more than absolutely necessary and strictly proportionate.

105.  The Court reiterates that the text of Article 2 of the Convention, read as a whole, demonstrates that paragraph 2 does not primarily define instances where it is permitted to intentionally kill an individual, but describes situations where it is permitted to “use force” which may result, as an unintended outcome, in the deprivation of life. The use of force, however, must be no more than “absolutely necessary” for the achievement of any of the purposes set out in subparagraphs (a), (b) or (c). In this respect the use of the term “absolutely necessary” in Article 2 § 2 indicates that a stricter and more compelling test of necessity must be employed than that normally applicable when determining whether State action is “necessary in a democratic society” under paragraph 2 of Articles 8-11 of the Convention. In particular, the force used must be strictly proportionate to the achievement of the aims set out in sub-paragraphs 2 (a), (b) and (c) of Article 2 of the Convention (see McCann and Others v. the United Kingdom, 27 September 1995, §§ 148-149, Series A no. 324).

CONCLUSION: Violation of Article 2 - Right to life (Article 2-1 - Life) (Substantive aspect);Violation of Article 2 - Right to life (Article 2-1 - Effective investigation) (Procedural aspect);No violation of Article 3 - Prohibition of torture (Article 3 - Degrading treatment) (Substantive aspect);Non-pecuniary damage - award (Article 41 - Non-pecuniary damage;Just satisfaction)
